   Business and Industry Commission Agenda Report

Meeting Date:  November 13, 2025
From:  Alice Hui, Director of Finance
Department:  Finance
Submitted by:  Alice Hui, Director of Finance

Subject
Potential Ballot Measure - Utility Users Tax

Recommendation
No action required by the Commission. This is a presentation only.

Background
The City’s existing 6% Utility Users Tax (UUT), passed by voters (Measure R) in 2018, is
scheduled to sunset in 2028 unless renewed by the voters. The UUT generates approximately
$14 million each year, which represents more than 15% of the City’s total revenues, making it
the City’s second largest revenue source. This revenue source is a vital component of the City’s
general fund and supports a wide range of essential services that keep the City functioning
effectively, including public safety such as fire protection, paramedic, 9-1-1 emergency response,
police and crime prevention, as well as the cleaning and maintenance of streets, sidewalks,
infrastructure, and public facilities.

UUTs are taxes levied by local governments on the consumption of utility services, including
electricity, gas, water, sewer, telecommunications, sanitation, and cable television. Currently,
nearly 156 cities in California levy UUT, with rates typically ranging between 1% and 11%. The
average rate in Los Angeles County is 6%. The City’s UUT applies to utility services used by
commercial and industrial customers, including telephone, electricity, gas, water, fiber, cable,
and video services, but excludes residential users.

The City’s UUT was first adopted by voters in 2013 (Measure M) at a 1% rate to stabilize financial
conditions and support essential services. However, the revenue generated was not sufficient to
fund the essential services provided by the City, forcing the City to rely on transfers from its
utilities to bridge the gap. To ensure long-term fiscal stability, voters approved an increase to 6%
in 2018 with a ten (10) year sunset clause.

Due to its unique industrial structure, the City does not benefit from the traditional levels of
property or sales tax revenues that most municipalities rely on. Furthermore, this fiscal constraint
is compounded by the way state and federal transportation funding is allocated. Road and street
improvement dollars are typically allocated based on residential population, leaving cities like
Vernon, despite its large industrial and business community, consistently underfunded. As a
result, the UUT serves as one of the few reliable sources of revenue that the City can depend on
to provide high-quality essential services.

Analysis
The City’s current general fund budget is $95 million, funding public safety – police & fire, health,
public works, capital improvements, and other essential services. The $14 million in UUT revenue
supports 15% of this budget. Without this revenue source, the City would face a significant fiscal
gap and budget shortfall, making it difficult to provide vital services and programs for residents
and businesses. This would necessitate reductions in core services, suspension of capital
projects, or the pursuit of alternative revenue sources.

 The table below illustrates an across-the-board reduction for each General Fund department.
Since the fire services are contracted with Los Angeles County and cannot be reduced, the
remaining departments would be subject to a 20% reduction:

 Public Safety - Fire  24,168,393  -

 General Government  18,972,722  (3,752,090)

To provide perspective, the reduction required in the Police Department may equate to the
elimination of up to 20 sworn officers, representing nearly half of the current force. Such a
reduction would significantly impair the City’s ability to provide essential public safety services.
Similarly, reductions within the Health Department would adversely affect the timeliness and
effectiveness of health regulations and inspections, thereby diminishing the City’s capacity to
safeguard community health. The City is also responsible for maintaining 47 miles of streets and
88 miles of sewers and storm drains. Any reduction in Public Works staffing or resources would
severely hinder the City’s ability to maintain critical infrastructure, including streets, traffic signals,
sewer and storm drain systems, and graffiti abatement. Current revenue constraints have already
resulted in deferred street maintenance; further reductions would exacerbate this situation and
prove detrimental to overall infrastructure conditions. Additionally, the City’s sewer system is
approaching the end of its useful life, creating an urgent need for capital replacement. Because
the City does not assess sewer fees, funding for this replacement must come entirely from the
General Fund, placing an even greater strain on limited resources.

Action Plan and Next Steps
Because the UUT is time-limited and requires voter renewal to remain in effect, placing the
measure on the April 2026 ballot allows the City to proactively prepare for its 2028 sunset. This
will provide sufficient time for community engagement to clearly communicate the importance of
maintaining this critical revenue source. To support this effort, staff issued a Request for
Proposals (RFP) on March 24, 2025 for Ballot Measure Outreach & Consulting Services and
Public Opinion Polling Services. Team CivX in partnership with True North Research were
determined to be the most qualified and capable firms to meet the City’s needs. Both firms have
extensive experience working with cities throughout California on similar ballot measures.

On October 21, 2025 the City Council received a presentation on a potential UUT ballot measure
for the April 2026 Municipal Election. An informational meeting on the UUT is planned for
December 4, 2025. Staff plans to bring the general election resolution to the City Council on
November 18, 2025 followed by the UUT ballot measure resolution on December 16, 2025.
Fiscal Impact
There is no fiscal impact associated with this report. The UUT revenue has an approximately $14
million impact annually to the City’s General Fund.

  Recommendation: Receive and file the report on the Vernon Public Utilities Water Rate
  Study.

  Public Utilities General Manager Dusenberry presented the staff report and
  accompanying PowerPoint presentation along with Public Utilities Finance Manager,
  Richard Corbi and NewGen Strategies Partner, Eric Callocchia.

Item 2  Page 17 of 19
 Special Business and Industry Commission Meeting Minutes  Page 3 of 4
October 2, 2025

  The Commission expressed interest in prospective growth and usage for the new data
  centers and hydrogen plant, and the revenue loss of the mentioned top-ten user
  (rPlanet Earth). Staff explained the prospective usage of the clean hydrogen and data
  centers would increase load, but combined, would not replace the usage of Farmer
  John.

  Public Utilities General Manager Dusenberry explained one of the reasons behind
  Vernon’s water rates being low in comparison to other agencies is that the utility
  understands the water rate directly hits businesses’ bottom line, and the increase
  actually supports the utility keeping the rates lower in comparison to the expensive and
  uncontrollable cost of importing water.

  Staff provided information on reclaimed water usage and demand, and explained
  reclaimed water used at the power plant is provided by Central Basin and the use of
  reclaimed water could be expanded in the future, noting that the reclaimed water
  system is not built out, and the price of building the infrastructure would be costly.

  Staff explained the transfer from the Electric Fund to the Water Fund is capped at $15
  million, and the imported water cost and average noted in the presentation is over the
  past 5 years.

  In response to questions from the Commission on the availability of ground water in
  drought conditions, staff explained in past droughts, Vernon’s ground water wells met
  the water usage demands without having to import water adding Vernon’s ground water
  wells have supplied 100% of the water in Vernon since November 2020 and, although
  Central Basin’s water connection valves are routinely flushed, they are exercised as a
  back-up water source for the City.

  Staff explained ground water well depths and prospective treatment plans, a minor
  detection for PFAS, grant funding availability, briefed on lawsuit settlement fund
  sources, and expanded on information on the process of recharging ground water wells
  which are mainly performed by Public Works operations through different storm water
  capture systems, and new construction development requirements.

  Staff explained the proposed water rate does not include taxes or other fees such as
  pass-through fees.

  In response to the Commission’s interest in incentivizing big businesses and large
  water consumers to the City, Staff explained the utility applies the rate objectively and
  evenly to large and small users alike. Staff added that Vernon has ownership rights to
  all the ground water in Vernon and has the capacity to provide water service to any size
  business such as the former dye-houses that were formerly located in Vernon.

  Staff provided information on the proposed rate-roll out plan to perform outreach and
  opportunity for the public to make comments would be somewhat flexible, would include

4.  Brief Reports, Announcements, or Directives to Staff
  City Administrator Saeki announced that in support of the Vernon community workers
  and businesses, the City has created a webpage dedicated to immigration and
  enforcement resources and has partnered with CHIRLA (Coalition for Humane
  Immigrant Rights) to provide legal support services and education. He added that
  CHIRLA would be hosting weekly virtual immigration training sessions for Vernon
  businesses and workers every Thursday at 3 p.m. alternating week to week in English
  and Spanish.

  He also announced October is “Pink Patch Project Month” recognizing breast cancer
  awareness during the month of October. Chief Sousa has authorized uniformed
  personnel to wear pink patches throughout the month of October to raise funds for the
  Pink Patch Project, an organization dedicated to raising breast cancer awareness and
  supporting research and prevention. He added this year’s Pink Patch Project gear
  would be available for sale to the public; patches would be available to purchase for
  $10 and Pink Patch Project t-shirts would be available to purchase for $20. Anyone
  interested in purchasing patches and t-shirts could contact Detective Gonzalez at
  ext.123, and all proceeds would benefit the Pink Patch Project.

  PRESENTATIONS
  1.  Potential Ballot Measure - Utility Users Tax
  Recommendation:
  No action required by the Commission. This is a presentation only.

  Finance Director/City Treasurer Hui presented the staff report.

  The Commission discussed building department inspections and in particular, concerns
  about consistency over fire inspection service deliveries from a budget standpoint,
  considering one previous inspector handled the entire City, and now, each of the three
  inspectors handle three different areas of Vernon. Staff confirmed there was previously
  one Vernon Fire Inspector who provided fire inspections to the entire city, and the
  current model of Los Angeles County Fire Department, provides for three LA County
  Fire Department Fire Inspectors who are responsible for conducting fire inspections on
  building developments. Staff informed the Commission that there are efforts being
  made through ongoing meetings to discuss concerns brought forth by both the City and
  by LA County Fire Chiefs over service deliveries and inspection-related responsibilities.

  The Commission discussed the sunset of the current 6% utility users tax, the evolution
  of the utility user’s taxation over time, and expressed concerns over it potentially
  evolving into a permanent funding source. The Commission expressed their preference
  to have staff present flexible options to the 6% rate and explore proposing a sunset
  date. Staff confirmed the sunset of the current tax is 2028, and relayed concerns on
  global impacts surrounding the utility user tax as it relates to the whole organization,
  and affirmed staff have contingency plans in place in the event the measure does not
  pass. The Commission expressed a desire to have staff to include and engage
  businesses in conversations through a series of informational meetings over an
  extended period of time and to provide in-depth analyses with comparative data to
  surrounding cities.

  In response to questions from the Commission, staff provided information on electric
  revenue shortfalls, impacts to local businesses who must weigh the costs to conduct
  business in California, and the recent efforts to leverage state and federal legislative
  support through a memorandum of understanding with five neighboring cities, newly
  known as “The Big Five” with the goal to garner support to fund capital infrastructure
  projects for smaller cities in the LA area, like Vernon.

  The Commission expressed their desire to be provided with the opportunity to give
  feedback and make recommendations to the City Council through the commission
  discussion and recommendation process. Staff assured the Commission that their
  significant concerns and considerations regarding the potential ballot measure for utility
